analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal tax credits that subsidize wind, solar, and other renewable energy projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal renewable energy tax credits was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate two long-standing federal tax credits: one that pays renewable electricity producers for each unit of power they generate, and one that covers a share of the cost of building renewable energy projects, with the repeal applied retroactively to the end of 2021 [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Representative Scott Perry in February 2022, sent to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, fossil fuel power producers (coal, oil, and natural gas) would have gained ground against wind and solar competitors that currently receive federal tax support [S2] [S3]. Federal taxpayers would have benefited from lower government spending on the credits, though that saving would come from taxing renewable projects that are now largely untaxed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would strike the production tax credit (section 45), which pays renewable electricity producers for each kilowatt-hour generated, and the investment tax credit (section 48), which covers a share of the cost of building renewable energy facilities [S3].

Repeal would take effect for electricity produced and sold after December 31, 2021, and for taxable years beginning after that date, eliminating future federal subsidy payments to renewable generators [S3].
Removing the credits would reduce federal tax expenditures and put unsubsidized fossil generation on more equal tax footing with renewables, which is the benefit sought by the bill's supporters.

analysis.who_pays: Wind and solar developers would lose credits that offset a substantial share of project costs, raising the price of building new renewable capacity [S2] [S3]. Because the repeal applies retroactively to projects with taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 [S3], projects already under construction would have been hit mid-stream. Homeowners and businesses installing solar would pay more, and, over time, the slower shift away from fossil generation could leave electricity customers facing higher prices and more pollution.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wind and solar developers and installers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the credits would raise the cost of wind and solar projects — the credits are the principal federal subsidy for renewable generation — likely slowing the buildout of cleaner electricity sources [S2].
The retroactive effective date of December 31, 2021 [S3] would have penalized projects already under way, an abrupt change that even supporters of trimming energy subsidies generally avoid.

The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill saves federal revenue only by withdrawing support that the wind and solar industries' business models are built around, which risks jobs and investment in those sectors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one clear benefit is federal savings from ending two energy tax expenditures. Its cost falls on renewable energy development: less wind and solar built, higher upfront costs for households and businesses that install it, and a slower transition away from fossil generation. The retroactive effective date makes the change harsher than a simple phase-out, and the bill offered no transition for projects already in the pipeline. On balance it is a targeted gift to competing fossil generators more than a fiscal reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Perry introduced the bill on February 8, 2022.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, February 8, 2022.
Three House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, but the bill attracted no further action.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, floor vote, or any other step after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wind and solar developers and the homeowners and businesses that install renewable energy are better off, because the credits that offset their costs remain on the books. Fossil fuel generators gained nothing from the repeal they supported.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wind and solar developers and installers

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the renewable production and investment tax credits.

for.name: Three House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; it sat in committee from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll calls exist; all four members attached to it — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat supported it.

industries.note: The bill would strip the production and investment tax credits that offset a large share of the cost of building wind and solar projects, raising project costs and slowing construction [S3]. If the bill had passed, cleaner and often cheaper electricity would reach consumers more slowly.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas power producers
industries.note: Repeal would end the federal subsidies that give renewables an edge, improving fossil generators' competitive position. Their gain would come at the expense of a faster shift to cleaner energy, which ordinary electricity customers and taxpayers' health interests favor.

The investment tax credit directly reduces the price tag for homeowners and businesses installing solar; repeal would remove it for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, raising customer costs and cutting sales.
